assessment.nobel_worthiness: The heterogeneous-firm framework changed how trade is modelled. It explains selection into exporting, within-industry reallocation and a new channel for gains from trade. It also redirected a large empirical literature and is used in policy work. Foundational conceptual change, broad influence, and sustained empirical support.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the central contribution. Helpman has a long record on trade with increasing returns and firm-level heterogeneity, including work with Melitz and Yeaple. Redding is influential on quantitative and spatial extensions but is more of a second-generation contributor, so he is left out.
assessment.maturity: More than two decades of confirmation, with extensive firm-level data tests and many extensions. Well past the point where the core insight could be called provisional.
uncertainties: Krugman's 2008 prize partly overlaps in subject matter, though it covers a different mechanism.
Credit overlaps with Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum on exporter heterogeneity, who are not on this list.
Some predictions, such as the Pareto-distribution results, are sensitive to functional-form assumptions.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Kiyotaki and Moore's credit-cycles model shows how collateral values and borrowing constraints amplify and propagate shocks. It underpins the modern macro-finance treatment of financial frictions. Its relevance was shown by the 2008 crisis and its aftermath.
assessment.attribution: Kiyotaki and Moore (1997) is the core, with a clear two-author attribution. Gertler and Gilchrist are important for the financial accelerator and its empirical side, but that branch overlaps heavily with Bernanke, who is already a laureate. Restricting to two names keeps the credit clean.
assessment.maturity: Nearly thirty years of use, and the mechanism is now standard in macro-finance and policy models. Empirical evidence on collateral channels is substantial, though identification varies by setting.
uncertainties: Bernanke-Gertler contributions and the 2022 banking prize for Bernanke, Diamond and Dybvig may be seen as covering part of this ground.
Quantitative support for the amplification magnitude is debated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The alternating-offers bargaining model gave a tractable, strategic foundation for bargaining and a unique subgame-perfect outcome. It is now a building block in labour, industrial organisation, political economy and monetary models. This is a long-recognised foundational theory contribution.
assessment.attribution: Rubinstein (1982) is the central paper and its authorship is unambiguous. Wolinsky and Binmore contributed important extensions and links to markets and to the Nash program, but their contributions are more derivative. A single-laureate proposal reflects that clarity.
assessment.maturity: More than four decades of use. It is secure as theory, so the question is timing and priority within game theory, not confirmation.
uncertainties: Game theory has already been recognised several times, which may raise the threshold.
Binmore and Wolinsky are not credited in the proposal, and a committee might prefer a broader trio.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Bayesian persuasion and information design give a general framework for how a sender should shape information to influence decisions. It unifies and extends cheap talk, disclosure and mechanism design. It has been applied in markets, regulation, politics and platform design.
assessment.attribution: Kamenica and Gentzkow (2011) is the foundational paper. Morris, with Bergemann, developed the robust, general information-design framework, so he is a strong third name. Bergemann is a plausible alternative to Morris.
assessment.maturity: The core idea is about fifteen years old. Theoretical uptake is rapid and empirical or experimental testing is growing but limited, so it is somewhat early compared with the older candidates.
uncertainties: Experimental and field support for sender-optimal persuasion is thin and mixed.
The choice between Morris and Bergemann for the third slot is uncertain.
It may be judged premature.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The work builds large-scale administrative-data measurement of intergenerational mobility, neighbourhood effects and place-based determinants of opportunity. It has changed the evidence base for public policy debates. Its contribution is partly measurement and data infrastructure, and partly causal evidence on neighbourhood effects.
assessment.attribution: Chetty leads the programme. Hendren is central to the neighbourhood-effects and exposure work. Friedman and Katz are major collaborators, with Katz also known for the earlier Moving to Opportunity work. Large team authorship makes the individual shares hard to separate.
assessment.maturity: Mostly from the past ten to fifteen years. Findings have been widely replicated in other countries and datasets, though some neighbourhood-causal estimates have been challenged on methods and robustness.
uncertainties: Team and collaborator attribution is diffuse.
Some mobility measures and the causal interpretation of place effects remain contested.
It may be early for a laureate recognition.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The task-based view of technology and the China-shock work changed understanding of how automation and trade reshape labour demand, wages and local labour markets. The work has strong policy relevance and has been highly influential in empirical labour and trade.
assessment.attribution: Autor is central to both the task-based and trade-shock strands. Hanson and Dorn are central to the China-shock identification. Acemoglu and Restrepo, who also developed the task framework, are not on this list and are a significant overlapping claim. Katz is credited here for earlier work on skill-biased change.
assessment.maturity: About fifteen years of work, with extensive replication and extension. Robustness is better than for many policy-relevant results, although some magnitudes and identification choices are debated.
uncertainties: Overlap with other task-based work not credited here complicates attribution.
Debate persists over exposure measurement and the size of effects.
It is unclear whether the trade and technology strands should be recognised together.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Nominal rigidities, the New Keynesian Phillips curve and policy-rule analysis form the framework most central banks use. The influence on practice and on the structure of modern macroeconomics is very large.
assessment.attribution: Credit is spread over many people: Calvo on staggered pricing, Taylor on staggered contracts and the policy rule, Woodford on the synthesis, and Gali, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Smets and Gertler on estimation and extensions. Any three-name selection is arbitrary at the margin, and this is the main weakness.
assessment.maturity: Decades of use in practice. Some components, notably the Phillips-curve fit, were challenged during the post-2020 inflation, though the framework remains standard.
uncertainties: The three-laureate limit makes it hard to represent the full set of contributors fairly.
Whether the committee would prefer a narrower, better-defined component.
Empirical fit of New Keynesian pricing was questioned in recent inflation episodes.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Methods for estimating heterogeneous treatment effects and debiased or double machine learning allow valid inference with high-dimensional data. They are widely adopted in applied microeconomics, policy evaluation and experimentation, with a clear methodological advance.
assessment.attribution: Chernozhukov, with co-authors, developed double or debiased machine learning. Athey, with Imbens and Wager, developed causal forests and related treatment-effect methods. Imbens is already a laureate, which complicates credit. Wager is credited on causal forests but is a more junior contributor.
assessment.maturity: The main methods date from roughly 2015 to 2018 and are spreading quickly. Time is still needed to see which methods endure and how they perform across applications.
uncertainties: Maturity is the main concern, and the pace of methodological change is high.
Authorship overlaps with Imbens and Newey and others outside this list.
Practical performance in finite samples and with weak overlap varies.
